newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks expected to head higher in early trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks expected to head higher in early trade.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to kick off inaugural day trading on the upside but volume will be slim as bonds will not be in play.
The bond market is closed for Martin Luther King Jr Day, a federal holiday. The stock market will remain open.

"This is a holiday so it will be quiet relative to last week," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "We will be steady at the open and then we have to see whether we keep the forward momentum."
The Dow closed above 6800 for the first time Friday.

Wachtel said that in addition to the absence of a bond market, Wall Street will be subdued as attention will be diverted to the inauguration of President Bill Clinton for a second term in Washington D.C.

He said that the market would be looking at Microsoft Corp which reported a strong quarter after the close of trading Friday but was down overnight in London after the company warned of slower earnings growth next year.
"Whenever Microsoft gives a press conference they are conservative about the future," he said, adding that he did not expect the stock to take too bad of a beating.
"Wall Street knows Microsoft's body language, and I don't think that anyone will get too excited over it," he said.
Nasdaq will begin trading on Monday under new rules which will reduce the number of shares that can be traded, said Nasdaq spokesman Reid Walker.
The minimum limit order quote size will be cut to 100 shares from the previous 1,000. It will be applied on a pilot basis on the 50 most active stocks traded on Nasdaq.
Other Nasdaq-listed issues will be phased in over the next eight months.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 610 points at 17,480.
In London, the FTSE 100 was down seven points at 4201.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, Microsoft was down 1-1/8 at 86. Shares of International Business Machines Corp were down 1/2 at 164-3/4 while Intel Corp was down 1/2 at 143-5/8.
The dollar was firm in Europe wheile profit-taking trimmed its gains in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly slightly higher, with the long bond up 1/32 to yield 6.83 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that it's been nine months since Roger Enrico took over as chief executive of PepsiCo Inc amid starry expectations for the food and beverage conglomerate.
Instead, Enrico has been faced with massive losses at Pepsi's Latin American bottler and sluggish sales at the fast food business.
